content.title: Globalisation & Business

body.text: **Globalisation** is the increasing integration and interdependence of the world's economies through the free flow of goods, services, capital, and labour across borders. For businesses, it means both wider opportunities and fiercer competition.

Three forces drive it. **Technology** — the internet, containerised shipping, and digital payments make it cheap to coordinate supply chains across continents. **Trade liberalisation** — the WTO and bilateral agreements reduce tariffs and quotas, lowering the cost of cross-border trade. **Deregulation** — governments opening financial markets and relaxing FDI restrictions invite foreign capital and competition.

For businesses the impact is double-edged. Globalisation opens **larger markets** and access to **cheaper inputs** (labour, raw materials, components), but it also brings **increased competition** from foreign firms and exposure to **foreign exchange risk** as revenues and costs span multiple currencies.

steps: Deregulation opens markets to foreign firms
body.result: Businesses access global markets but face global competition and FX risk

sections.title: Drivers of Globalisation
sections.keyIdea: Globalisation is driven by technology, trade liberalisation, and deregulation — together they shrink the effective distance between markets and allow firms to source, produce, and sell worldwide.
sections.examMatters: Examiners expect you to distinguish between the drivers (technology, liberalisation, deregulation) and the impacts on business (larger markets, cheaper inputs, competition, FX risk). A strong answer links a specific driver to a specific business outcome with a named example.

realExample.text: Zara's parent company Inditex operates a global supply chain spanning 12 countries, using advanced logistics technology to move garments from design to store in under two weeks. Cheap shipping and liberalised trade allow Zara to source fabric in Turkey, cut in Morocco, and sell in 96 markets worldwide.

sections.misconception: Students say globalisation only benefits large firms. Wrong — small firms can now sell globally through platforms like Amazon and Etsy, and source cheaply from Alibaba. Instead write: globalisation benefits firms of all sizes, though larger firms are better positioned to manage FX risk and regulatory complexity across multiple markets.

body.text: Globalisation reshapes business strategy in fundamental ways. Firms can **offshore** production to low-cost countries, **outsource** non-core functions to specialists abroad, and access a **global talent pool**. These choices lower costs but create supply chain dependencies and reputational risks.

Pricing becomes more complex because firms must account for **exchange rate fluctuations**, **transfer pricing** across subsidiaries, and different **price elasticities** in different markets. A strong pound makes UK exports expensive abroad; a weak pound makes imported inputs costly.

Risk management becomes critical. Firms use **hedging** (forward contracts to lock in exchange rates), **diversification** across markets, and **local sourcing** to reduce exposure. The most successful global firms balance efficiency (centralised production) with resilience (diversified supply chains).

steps: Revenue and costs in multiple currencies
body.result: Firms hedge, diversify, and localise to manage global risk

sections.title: Impact of Globalisation on Business Strategy
sections.keyIdea: Globalisation forces firms to rethink every strategic decision — from where they produce, to how they price, to how they manage currency exposure across borders.
sections.examMatters: A top-mark answer evaluates whether the benefits of globalisation (lower costs, larger markets) outweigh the risks (FX exposure, supply chain fragility, reputational risk) for a specific firm in a specific context. Always consider: 'It depends on the firm's size, industry, and risk appetite.'

realExample.text: Walmart's entry into India required adapting to local regulations that restricted FDI in multi-brand retail. Walmart initially used a joint venture with Bharti Enterprises to navigate rules, then shifted to wholesale cash-and-carry operations — showing how globalisation demands strategic flexibility, not just cost-cutting.

sections.misconception: Students assume globalisation means firms should always produce in the cheapest country. Wrong — supply chain disruption, quality control, and reputational damage from poor labour conditions can outweigh cost savings. Instead write: location decisions balance cost advantages against supply chain resilience, quality control, and ethical considerations.

takeaway: Three drivers: technology, trade liberalisation, deregulation — each lowers barriers to cross-border business.
Business impacts: larger markets and cheaper inputs, but more competition and FX risk.
Strategy must balance efficiency (offshoring, centralisation) with resilience (diversification, hedging).
Globalisation affects firms of all sizes — small firms access global platforms, large firms manage complex supply chains.

content.title: Trade Blocs

body.text: A **free trade area (FTA)** eliminates tariffs between members but each country keeps its own external tariffs on non-members. NAFTA (now USMCA) is a classic example — Mexico, the US, and Canada trade freely among themselves but set independent tariffs on imports from China.

A **customs union** goes further: members adopt a **common external tariff (CET)** against non-members, which simplifies trade rules but removes individual tariff policy. The EU began as a customs union — all members charge the same tariff on, say, Vietnamese textiles.

A **single market** adds the free movement of **capital and labour** alongside goods and services. The EU single market allows a Polish engineer to work in Germany without a visa and a French bank to operate in Spain without separate authorisation. For businesses inside, it creates a seamless domestic-style market of 450 million consumers.

steps: Customs union adds common external tariff
Single market adds free movement of labour and capital
body.result: Deeper integration = more trade but less national policy independence

sections.title: Types of Trade Blocs: FTA, Customs Union, Single Market
sections.keyIdea: Trade blocs range from free trade areas to full single markets — each deeper level of integration removes more barriers but demands more policy surrender from member states.
sections.examMatters: Examiners test your ability to rank the levels of integration and explain the trade-offs. A strong answer explains why deeper integration benefits businesses (larger barrier-free market) but constrains governments (cannot set independent trade policy).

realExample.text: BMW benefits hugely from the EU single market. It sources components from 15+ EU countries tariff-free, moves skilled engineers between plants in Germany, Austria, and the UK (pre-Brexit), and sells finished cars across 27 member states without customs paperwork or regulatory duplication.

sections.misconception: Students confuse a customs union with a single market. Wrong — a customs union only harmonises trade in goods with a common external tariff; a single market also allows free movement of services, capital, and labour. Instead write: a single market is a customs union plus the free movement of all factors of production.

body.text: **Trade creation** occurs when bloc membership replaces expensive domestic production with cheaper imports from a partner country. A Spanish wine producer gains tariff-free access to Germany, undercutting less efficient German vineyards — consumers benefit from lower prices.

**Trade diversion** occurs when the CET forces firms to switch from a cheaper non-member supplier to a more expensive bloc member. If the EU's CET makes Brazilian orange juice costlier than Spanish juice, UK buyers switch to Spain even though Brazil produces more cheaply — a net efficiency loss.

For businesses **inside** the bloc, the impact is overwhelmingly positive: barrier-free access to a huge market, simplified regulation, and larger customer bases. For businesses **outside**, the CET creates a competitive disadvantage that may force them to set up production inside the bloc (tariff-jumping FDI) to remain competitive.

body.result: Firms inside benefit; firms outside face new barriers or relocate

sections.title: Trade Creation, Trade Diversion & the Impact on Firms
sections.keyIdea: Trade blocs create trade among members by removing barriers, but they divert trade away from efficient non-members who face the CET — so not all trade effects are positive for global efficiency.
sections.examMatters: A common exam question asks you to evaluate whether joining a trade bloc benefits a country's businesses. Structure your answer: trade creation benefits (lower costs, bigger markets) vs trade diversion costs (losing efficient non-member suppliers) — then conclude with 'it depends on the relative size of creation vs diversion'.

realExample.text: Post-Brexit, UK fisheries lost tariff-free access to the EU single market. Scottish salmon exporters now face customs checks and paperwork delays that add cost and reduce freshness — a real-world example of trade diversion as EU buyers increasingly switch to Norwegian salmon (Norway has an EEA arrangement).

sections.misconception: Students assume trade blocs always increase total trade. Wrong — trade diversion can reduce global efficiency by redirecting purchases away from the cheapest producer. Instead write: trade blocs increase trade among members (creation) but may reduce trade with more efficient outsiders (diversion); the net effect depends on the size of each effect.

takeaway: FTA < customs union < single market — each level integrates more but surrenders more policy autonomy.
Trade creation replaces costly domestic output with cheaper partner imports — a net gain.
Trade diversion replaces cheap non-member imports with costlier member imports — a net loss.
Firms inside a bloc benefit from barrier-free access; firms outside may need tariff-jumping FDI to compete.

quiz.question: Which of the following best describes an emerging economy?
quiz.explanation: Emerging economies are characterised by rapid industrialisation, rising incomes and growing integration into global markets — they sit between developed and developing economies.

GDP per capita
Human Development Index (HDI)
Balance of payments
quiz.question: Which indicator combines income, health and education to measure development?
quiz.explanation: The HDI is a composite measure that combines income per capita, life expectancy and education levels to give a broader picture of development than GDP alone.

Increased unit costs for domestic producers

quiz.question: What is a key risk of over-specialisation in international trade?
quiz.explanation: Over-specialisation makes an economy dependent on a narrow range of exports — if demand falls or prices drop, the entire economy suffers.

Increasing the volume of imports
Preventing dumping by foreign firms
Safeguarding domestic jobs
quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason for protectionism?
quiz.explanation: Protectionism aims to restrict imports, not increase them. Governments use tariffs, quotas and subsidies to protect domestic producers from foreign competition.

options: Increased trade between bloc members leading to lower prices
Trade shifting from efficient non-members to less efficient bloc members
The removal of all tariffs between trading partners

quiz.question: What is trade diversion in the context of trading blocs?
quiz.explanation: Trade diversion occurs when a trading bloc causes trade to shift from more efficient non-member producers to less efficient member-state producers.

It eliminated the need for international trade agreements
It replaced air freight as the primary transport method
quiz.question: How has containerisation contributed to globalisation?
quiz.explanation: Containerisation standardised shipping and dramatically reduced transport costs, making global supply chains economically viable.

quiz.question: Which organisation's primary role is to promote free trade and resolve trade disputes?
quiz.explanation: The WTO promotes free trade by negotiating tariff reductions, setting trade rules and resolving trade disputes between member nations.

quiz.question: A government provides subsidies to domestic steel producers to help them compete with cheaper imports. This is an example of:
quiz.explanation: Domestic subsidies give financial assistance to home producers, lowering their costs and enabling them to compete with cheaper foreign imports — a form of protectionism.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of the EU single market?
quiz.explanation: The EU single market allows free movement of goods, services, capital and labour among member states. Not all members use the euro, and tax and wage policies remain national.

options: Increased demand for their products abroad
Lower production costs due to cheaper inputs
Reduced international sales and revenue

quiz.question: What is the most likely impact of retaliatory tariffs on exporting businesses?
quiz.explanation: When trading partners impose retaliatory tariffs, they raise the price of a country's exports, reducing demand and sales revenue for exporting businesses.

practice.guidance: Identify two causes such as: advances in communication technology (internet, mobile technology) reducing barriers to international trade, reduction in trade barriers through WTO negotiations and regional trading blocs, improvements in transportation (containerisation, cheaper air freight) reducing costs of moving goods, liberalisation of capital markets allowing freer movement of investment, growth of multinational corporations seeking new markets and lower production costs. For each, explain the mechanism by which it has accelerated globalisation.
practice.question: Explain two causes of increased globalisation over the past 30 years.

practice.context: SolarTech is a Chinese solar panel manufacturer that exports 60% of its output to the European Union. The EU has recently imposed a 25% tariff on imported solar panels from China, citing unfair subsidies.
practice.guidance: Analyse negative impacts on SolarTech: the tariff increases the price of its panels in the EU market, making them less competitive against European manufacturers; export volumes are likely to fall; revenue and profit from EU sales will decline; the company may need to absorb some of the tariff to remain competitive, reducing profit margins. Analyse possible strategic responses: establishing manufacturing within the EU to avoid tariffs (FDI), redirecting exports to non-EU markets, challenging the tariff through WTO dispute resolution, partnering with a European firm. Consider whether the tariff benefits or harms EU consumers who face higher solar panel prices.
practice.question: Analyse the impact of protectionist trade policies on SolarTech's operations.

practice.context: A developing country in Southeast Asia has recently joined a regional free trade agreement, removing tariffs on goods traded between member nations. The country's economy relies heavily on agriculture and low-cost manufacturing.
practice.guidance: Assess benefits: access to larger export markets for agricultural and manufactured goods, attracts foreign direct investment from multinational companies seeking low-cost production, lower prices for imported goods benefit consumers, technology transfer from foreign firms improves productivity, specialisation in areas of comparative advantage. Assess drawbacks: domestic industries may be unable to compete with more efficient foreign producers, infant industries may be destroyed before they develop, risk of over-dependence on a few export commodities, MNCs may exploit low labour standards, profits repatriated rather than reinvested locally, environmental damage from rapid industrialisation. Consider the specific context: agriculture may benefit from exports but could also be undercut by subsidised imports from wealthier nations. Make a judgement about whether the benefits outweigh the costs in the long run, considering the country's stage of development.
practice.question: Assess the extent to which free trade benefits developing countries.

practice.guidance: Explain that the WTO is an international body that sets rules for global trade, aims to reduce trade barriers between member nations, and provides a forum for negotiating trade agreements. Key roles include: administering trade rules and agreements, providing a dispute resolution mechanism for trade conflicts, monitoring national trade policies, and providing technical assistance to developing countries. Briefly note that it promotes free trade but has been criticised for slow progress in negotiations and for favouring developed nations.
practice.question: Explain the role of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in promoting international trade.

practice.guidance: Winners from globalisation: consumers benefit from lower prices and greater choice, businesses access larger markets and lower production costs, developing countries attract FDI and employment, cultural exchange and knowledge transfer, economic growth through increased trade and specialisation. Losers from globalisation: workers in developed countries face competition from low-wage economies (job losses in manufacturing), small domestic businesses cannot compete with MNCs, environmental degradation from increased production and transportation, cultural homogenisation and loss of local identity, growing income inequality both within and between countries, developing countries may become dependent on foreign investment. Evaluate the distribution of gains and losses: gains may be large in aggregate but unevenly distributed; the 'losers' (displaced workers, struggling local businesses) bear concentrated costs while the 'winners' (consumers, shareholders) enjoy diffuse benefits. Consider whether government policy can redistribute the gains to compensate the losers. Examine evidence from specific countries or industries. Reach a nuanced conclusion that avoids oversimplification and acknowledges that the impact depends on the specific context, policies, and institutions of each country.
practice.question: Evaluate the view that globalisation creates more winners than losers.
